newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to study floating heliport for U.S. military.
newsitem.headline: Japan to study floating heliport for U.S. military.

text.p: The governor of Japan's southernmost island of Okinawa said on Thursday he would allow the central government to conduct a feasibility study on the building of a floating heliport for use by the U.S. military.
The decision by Masahide Ota removed a major obstacle blocking the implementation of a Japan-U.S. agreement reached last December to streamline huge U.S. military bases on Okinawa.
Ota conveyed his decision to the mayor of Nago on the east coast of Okinawa, a key candidate location for the construction of the offshore heliport for the U.S. Marine Corps.
Top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama welcomed Ota's change of heart.
"This is a great step forward," Kajiyama told a regular news conference.
Ota had refused to accept any plan to build a heliport because it ran counter to the Okinawan view that the U.S. military on the island must be reduced and eventually removed.
Tokyo had agreed with Washington to build the heliport in exchange for vacating the Futenma Air Station in southern Okinawa.
The agreement followed a year of talks over a row triggered in September 1995 by the rape of an Okinawan schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen. The three are serving up to 10 years in a Japanese jail.

The United States agreed to hand back to Japan part or all of 11 military facilities on Okinawa, or roughly one-fifth of the 58,000 acres (23,500 hectares) occupied by the U.S. military on the subtropical island in the East China Sea.
There were no changes to the 28,000 military personnel, mostly U.S. Marines, stationed on Okinawa. More than 75 percent of all U.S. military facilities in Japan are on Okinawa.
